The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=14z for x≤0, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭RzdV

a
∫0π/2∫π/23π/2∫014cos⁡ϕρ3cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π/2∫π/23π/2∫014cos⁡ϕρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
 ∫0π/2∫π/23π/2∫014cos⁡ϕρ3cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫π/23π/2∫07cos⁡ϕρ3cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫π/23π/2∫07cos⁡ϕρ2cos⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 7 centered at (0,0,7).

With that in mind, let's now write the x2+y2+z2=14z in spherical polar coordinates:

x2+y2+z2=14zρ2=14ρcos⁡ϕρ(ρ−14cos⁡ϕ)=0

Since ρ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have ρ=14cos⁡ϕ.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤14cos⁡ϕ,π2≤θ≤3π2,0≤ϕ≤π2}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=z:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρcos⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭RzdV=∭Δρcos⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π/2∫π/23π/2∫014cos⁡ϕρ3cos⁡ϕsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Sphere
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/0cdaa9545b4e0688d23868f876187653ad01b95f59348d9b9121af9a55563380.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=14z$ for $x\le 0,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}z\,\text{d}V
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$  represents one-half of the sphere of radius $7$ centered at $(0,0,7).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=14z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =14z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =14\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -14\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =14\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/1d7643c7855d4de05e02036eb3ca452592d5feea6c09e4b37c2b84fbe4b440b5.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 14\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le \theta \le \frac{3\pi }{2},\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=z:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}z\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{14\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=4y, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭RxdV

b

decision.explanation: The sphere becomes ρ²=4ρ sinθ sinϕ, so 0≤ρ≤4 sinθ sinϕ, with 0≤θ≤π and 0≤ϕ≤π. Multiplying x=ρ cosθ sinϕ by the Jacobian ρ² sinϕ gives ρ³ cosθ sin²ϕ. This matches option b.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/41b5ff62b86d0cc7ce341a013f1815b7bb203f5b93cb52c525844f9bb93839b2.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4y,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V
$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =4\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/cc029278b96456462e746450c8feeb9c9ec6169a9b36f56915758ffcc1f8dd70.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 2 centered at (0,2,0).

With that in mind, let's now write the x2+y2+z2=4y in spherical polar coordinates:

x2+y2+z2=4yρ2=4ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕρ(ρ−4sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)=0

Since ρ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have ρ=4sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤4sin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,0≤θ≤π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=x:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭RxdV=∭Δρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π∫0π∫04sin⁡θsin⁡ϕρ3cos⁡θsin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Sphere
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/41b5ff62b86d0cc7ce341a013f1815b7bb203f5b93cb52c525844f9bb93839b2.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4y,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $2$ centered at $(0,2,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=4y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =4y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =4\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/cc029278b96456462e746450c8feeb9c9ec6169a9b36f56915758ffcc1f8dd70.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}x\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=6z, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π/2∫02π∫03cos⁡ϕρ4cos2⁡θsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π/2∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ2sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
 ∫0π/2∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ4sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ4sin2⁡θsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫02π∫03cos⁡ϕρ4sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit

decision.explanation: The sphere becomes ρ²=6ρ cosϕ, giving 0≤ρ≤6 cosϕ, 0≤ϕ≤π/2, and 0≤θ≤2π. Since x²+y²=ρ² sin²ϕ, multiplying by the Jacobian ρ² sinϕ gives ρ⁴ sin³ϕ. This matches option c.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/6502641896d838a55fea58ceba47c77b910bf7a2520f11e68c7bfebf4bc28559.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=6z,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $3$ centered at $(0,0,3).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=6z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =6z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =6\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/d13b86d76d7ca5f700c75bcc9f65da43bdc4da2b013ab30ec3033d5e4b05c5c8.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{4}{sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=6z, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭Rx2+y2dV

a
 ∫0π/2∫02π∫03cos⁡ϕρ4cos2⁡θsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π/2∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ2sin2⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
c
 ∫0π/2∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ4sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
 ∫0π∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ4sin2⁡θsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫0π∫02π∫03cos⁡ϕρ4sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 3 centered at (0,0,3).

With that in mind, let's now write the x2+y2+z2=6z in spherical polar coordinates:

x2+y2+z2=6zρ2=6ρcos⁡ϕρ(ρ−6cos⁡ϕ)=0

Since ρ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have ρ=6cos⁡ϕ.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤6cos⁡ϕ,0≤θ≤2π,0≤ϕ≤π2}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=x2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=ρ2sin2⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭Rx2+y2dV=∭Δρ2sin2⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫0π/2∫02π∫06cos⁡ϕρ4sin3⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Sphere
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/6502641896d838a55fea58ceba47c77b910bf7a2520f11e68c7bfebf4bc28559.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=6z,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $3$ centered at $(0,0,3).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=6z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =6z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =6\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/d13b86d76d7ca5f700c75bcc9f65da43bdc4da2b013ab30ec3033d5e4b05c5c8.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2} \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{6\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}{\rho }^{4}{sin}^{3}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Since √(x²+y²)=ρ sinϕ, multiplying its reciprocal by the Jacobian ρ² sinϕ gives ρ. The sphere gives 0≤ρ≤−12 cosϕ, with π/2≤ϕ≤π and 0≤θ≤2π. This matches option d.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/0aadb414e61f8a7e9d1ba1d47e10c2ba1e7b94b72155c0882a08e0121646f6f6.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-12z,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V
$$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $6$ centered at $(0,0,-6).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-12z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-12z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-12\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/a303436877fdc4559e7bdfc302f8660258ea6ee3cb46d9adb0eb961a1e889b27.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

The region R is enclosed inside the sphere x2+y2+z2=−12z, shown above. Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. ∭R1x2+y2dV

a
 ∫π/2π∫02π∫0−12cos⁡ϕ1ρsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
b
 ∫0π∫02π∫0−6cos⁡ϕρdρdθdϕ
c
 ∫0π∫02π∫0−12cos⁡ϕρsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
d
∫π/2π∫02π∫0−12cos⁡ϕρdρdθdϕ
e
 ∫π/2π∫02π∫0−6cos⁡ϕ1ρsin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents the sphere of radius 6 centered at (0,0,−6).

With that in mind, let's now write the x2+y2+z2=−12z in spherical polar coordinates:

x2+y2+z2=−12zρ2=−12ρcos⁡ϕρ(ρ+12cos⁡ϕ)=0

Since ρ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have ρ=−12cos⁡ϕ.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤−12cos⁡ϕ,0≤θ≤2π,π2≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=1x2+y2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=1(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2+(ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ)2=1ρ2sin2⁡ϕ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=1ρ2sin2⁡ϕ=1ρsin⁡ϕ

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

∭R1x2+y2dV=∭Δ1ρsin⁡ϕ⋅ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ=∫π/2π∫02π∫0−12cos⁡ϕρdρdθdϕ.

content.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Triple Integral Defined Over a Shifted Sphere
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/0aadb414e61f8a7e9d1ba1d47e10c2ba1e7b94b72155c0882a08e0121646f6f6.png)

The region $R$ is enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-12z,$ shown above. 
Express the following triple integral in spherical polar coordinates. 

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V
$$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $6$ centered at $(0,0,-6).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=-12z$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =-12z \\ {\rho }^{2} & =-12\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho +12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =-12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/a303436877fdc4559e7bdfc302f8660258ea6ee3cb46d9adb0eb961a1e889b27.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le -12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}+(\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{-12\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ}\rho \,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The radius is 5, and y≥0 gives 0≤θ≤π. In spherical coordinates the integrand including the Jacobian is 4ρ³ sinϕ. Thus the integral equals (∫₀⁵4ρ³ dρ)(∫₀πdθ)(∫₀πsinϕ dϕ)=625·π·2=1250π, matching option d.

$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the change of variables formula in the form

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∭Δf(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)ρ2sin⁡ϕdρdθdϕ.

If (ρ,θ,ϕ) are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates (x,y,z) can be found by using the following formulas:

x=ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,y=ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,z=ρcos⁡ϕ

Notice that the region R represents one-half of the sphere of radius 5 centered at the origin.

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as

Δ={(ρ,θ,ϕ):0≤ρ≤5,0≤θ≤π,0≤ϕ≤π}.

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function f(x,y,z)=4x2+y2+z2:

f(x,y,z)=f(ρcos⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρsin⁡θsin⁡ϕ,ρcos⁡ϕ)=4ρ2=4ρ

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/3358dd177a848ea569fdeab6e39f4be268cc7325bb01c788e9bfe2ea2145d1eb.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=25$ for $y\ge 0,$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $5$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/27304d8933e63e9edd2ad22fe937a9b37d05c6ae01569857e957bb1ebe5d73c0.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 5,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =4\sqrt{{\rho }^{2}} \\  & =4\rho \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain  

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}4\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}4\rho \cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{5}4{\rho }^{3}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi }\cdot [{\rho }^{4}]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =5} \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (\pi -0)\cdot ({5}^{4}-0) \\  & =1\,250\pi \end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The sphere gives 0≤ρ≤2 sinθ sinϕ, with 0≤θ≤π and 0≤ϕ≤π. The factor 1/ρ² cancels the Jacobian's ρ², leaving sinϕ. Integrating in ρ gives 2 sinθ sin²ϕ, so the integral is 2(∫₀π sinθ dθ)(∫₀π sin²ϕ dϕ)=2·2·(π/2)=2π, option e.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/53b96d29aaddea4971bc14207fa153613f2492b123c4de70d14161b3f6a17df8.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2y,$ shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =2y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =2\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/cd499dfb1a27171f56e9d253e42fec5884260adef1f8ca5e9e2cecd5a4fb45da.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ[\rho ]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ-0)\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & ={[ϕ-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =(\pi -0)\cdot (1+1) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Spherical Polar Coordinates
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/53b96d29aaddea4971bc14207fa153613f2492b123c4de70d14161b3f6a17df8.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2y,$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at $(0,1,0).$

With that in mind, let's now write the ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=2y$ in spherical polar coordinates:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2} & =2y \\ {\rho }^{2} & =2\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ \\ \rho (\rho -2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

 

Since $\rho $ cannot be identical to zero on the entire sphere, we must have $\rho =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/cd499dfb1a27171f56e9d253e42fec5884260adef1f8ca5e9e2cecd5a4fb45da.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,0\le \theta \le \pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\frac{1}{{\rho }^{2}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ[\rho ]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ}\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ-0)\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi }2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }2{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta  \\  & ={[ϕ-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =\pi } \\  & =(\pi -0)\cdot (1+1) \\  & =2\pi \end{aligned}
$$

$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Spherical Polar Coordinates
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/c7d87ad16ee6ab95b66bc2609707236c281407e473f5b834f484f002736c794c.png)

Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=9$ for $z\ge 0,$ shown above.
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents one-half of the sphere of radius $3$ centered at the origin.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14096572/assets/77791875e8b70bc528e4c765971d21c0567be80ffe58f7b1813d6be44db6bf33.png)

 

As a result, we obtain that in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \frac{\pi }{2}}.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}\,d\rho  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}1-\operatorname{cos}⁡2ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}{\rho }^{3}\,d\rho  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{[ϕ-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡2ϕ]}_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi /2}\cdot [-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot {[\frac{1}{4}{\rho }^{4}]}_{\rho =0}^{\rho =3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi }{2}-0)\cdot (-1+1)\cdot \frac{1}{4}(81-0) \\  & =\frac{\pi }{4}\cdot 0\cdot \frac{81}{4} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}3{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}3{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}3{\rho }^{2}{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}3{\rho }^{2}{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot [{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho  \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot ({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot (e-1) \\  & =4\pi (e-1)\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral by Converting to Spherical Polar Coordinates
content.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}3{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3/2}}\,\text{d}V
$$

over the region $R$ enclosed inside the sphere ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}=1.$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the change of variables formula in the form

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,dV={∭}_{Δ}\,f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ)\,{\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ.
$$

If $(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)$ are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates $(x,y,z)$ can be found by using the following formulas:

$$
x=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,y=\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\,z=\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ
$$

Notice that the region $R$ represents the sphere of radius $1$ centered at the origin. 
As a result, in spherical polar coordinates, our region can be expressed as 

$$
Δ={(\rho ,\theta ,ϕ)\,:\,0\le \rho \le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,\,0\le ϕ\le \pi }.
$$

Next, we substitute the spherical polar coordinates into the function $f(x,y,z)=3{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3/2}}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y,z) & =f(\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ,\rho \operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ) \\  & =3{e}^{({\rho }^{2})^{3/2}} \\  & =3{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}3{e}^{({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2})^{3}}\,\text{d}V & ={∭}_{Δ}3{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\cdot {\rho }^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}3{\rho }^{2}{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,d\rho \,d\theta \,dϕ \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡ϕ\,dϕ\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2\pi }d\theta \cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}3{\rho }^{2}{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}\,d\rho  \\  & =[-\operatorname{cos}⁡ϕ]_{ϕ=0}^{ϕ=\pi }\cdot [\theta ]_{\theta =0}^{\theta =2\pi }\cdot [{e}^{{\rho }^{3}}]_{\rho =0}^{\rho =1}\,d\rho  \\  & =-(-1-1)\cdot (2\pi -0)\cdot ({e}^{1}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2\cdot 2\pi \cdot (e-1) \\  & =4\pi (e-1)\end{aligned}
$$
